definition: Learning to rank (LTR) or machine-learned ranking (MLR) is the application of machine learning, often supervised, semi-supervised or reinforcement learning, in the construction of ranking models for information retrieval and recommender systems.
details: Training data may, for example, consist of lists of items with some partial order specified between items in each list. This order is typically induced by giving a numerical or ordinal score or a binary judgment (e.g. "relevant" or "not relevant") for each item. The goal of constructing the ranking model is to rank new, unseen lists in a similar way to rankings in the training data.

explainer.lead: Learning to rank builds models that order lists of items by learned relevance rather than by hand-tuned rules. It matters because search and recommendation quality depends on the order of results, not just on which items are retrieved.

tiers.eli5: It is like a coach who watches many judges rank contestants, learns what the judges tend to favour, and then orders new contestants the same way.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers train on lists with numeric, ordinal or binary relevance labels and optimize a ranking objective over whole lists, then apply the model to unseen queries. A common pitfall is training on labels that only weakly reflect real user preferences, so the model ranks well on paper but poorly in production.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, a ranking model f maps a query and a list of items to a ranking, learned from training lists where a partial order is given by scores or binary judgments, so that new lists are ordered similarly. Its quality depends on the training labels and on how well new queries resemble those seen in training.

explainer.example: A search team collects lists of ten documents per query, each judged relevant or not relevant, trains a model on those lists, and uses it to order documents for queries it has never seen.
